title: Detecting a nonreduced generic fibre after geometric-reduction preparation
statement: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a finite type morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], with $Y$ irreducible [def-weil-irreducible-components] and generic point $\eta$ [def-sc-generic-point]. Let $U\subseteq Y$ be a nonempty open subscheme, let $T$ be an integral scheme [def-pc-integral-scheme] with generic point $\xi$, and let $q:T\to U$ be a universal homeomorphism [def-weil-universal-homeomorphism]. Give $T$ its $Y$-scheme structure via the composite $T\xrightarrow{q}U\hookrightarrow Y$. Set $P=X\times_YT$, with projection $h:P\to T$ [def-pc-fibre-product], and $R=P_{\mathrm{red}}$ [def-weil-pbc-scheme-reduction], regarded as a $T$-scheme. Suppose $X_\eta$ is not geometrically reduced over $\kappa(\eta)$, whereas $R_\xi$ is geometrically reduced over $\kappa(\xi)$ [def-pc-scheme-fibre, def-weil-residue-field, def-pc-geometrically-irreducible]. Then the scheme $P_\xi$ is not reduced [def-pc-reduced-scheme].

proof.text: Put $g:T\to Y$ equal to $q$ followed by the open immersion. By the definition of universal homeomorphism, $q$ is a homeomorphism. Thus $q(\xi)$ is generic in $U$. Every nonempty open $W\subseteq Y$ meets $U$: otherwise the two proper closed complements of $W$ and $U$ cover the irreducible space $Y$. Hence $W\cap U$ contains $q(\xi)$, so $g(\xi)$ belongs to every nonempty open of $Y$ and is generic in $Y$. Uniqueness of the generic point of the scheme $Y$ gives $g(\xi)=\eta$.

source.place: Tag 0577, lemma-not-geometrically-reduced-in-neighbourhood, proof: the prepared generic points; elementary topological identification

proof.text: Suppose, for a contradiction, that $P_\xi$ is reduced. The integral scheme $T$ is irreducible, so its generic point $\xi$ is the generic point of its sole irreducible component. Apply reduction of generic fibres to $h:P\to T$: the canonical map $R_\xi\to P_\xi$ identifies $R_\xi$ with $(P_\xi)_{\mathrm{red}}$ over $\kappa(\xi)$. A reduced scheme has zero nilradical, so its reduction has the same structure sheaf and is canonically itself. Consequently $R_\xi\to P_\xi$ is an isomorphism over $\kappa(\xi)$. The assumed geometric reducedness of $R_\xi$ therefore makes $P_\xi$ geometrically reduced over $\kappa(\xi)$.

source.place: Tag 0577, lemma-not-geometrically-reduced-in-neighbourhood, proof: the reduction map on generic fibres; Tag 054Z, lemma-reduction-generic-fibre

proof.text: Choose algebraic closures of $\kappa(\xi)$ and $\kappa(\eta)$. The geometric fibre $P_{\bar\xi}$ is the base change of $P_\xi$ to the chosen closure of $\kappa(\xi)$, so it is reduced. Apply the geometric-reduced-fibre-locus base-change equality to $f:X\to Y$ and $g:T\to Y$, whose pullback is exactly $h:P\to T$. The equality at $\xi$, together with $g(\xi)=\eta$, says that $X_{\bar\eta}$ is reduced. This is the base change of $X_\eta$ to the chosen algebraic closure of $\kappa(\eta)$; the algebraic-closure test implies that $X_\eta$ is geometrically reduced over $\kappa(\eta)$. This contradicts the hypothesis. Therefore $P_\xi$ is not reduced.
